1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will act compassionately toward Jacob]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of the nation descended from the patriarch Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will act compassionately toward the people of Israel]

The expression **will be joined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the sojourner. Alternate translation: [And the sojourner will join himself]

2.note: In this sentence, the pronoun **they** refers to the house of Israel. The subject shifts back to the Israelites after the previous sentence had “peoples” as the subject. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites will be captors of their captors]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the word **captors** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And they will take captive those who once held them captive]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And Israel will take captive those who took them captive; indeed, they will rule over those who oppressed them]

3.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **And it will happen** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. See how you translated the similar expression in 10:12.

3.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֗ה בְּ⁠י֨וֹם הָנִ֤יחַ יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠ךָ֔ מֵֽ⁠עָצְבְּ⁠ךָ֖ וּ⁠מֵ⁠רָגְזֶ֑⁠ךָ וּ⁠מִן־הָ⁠עֲבֹדָ֥ה הַ⁠קָּשָׁ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עֻבַּד־בָּֽ⁠ךְ
3.note: This event does not happen right away but only after Yahweh gives the Israelites rest from their suffering. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After Yahweh gives rest to you from your pain and from your turmoil and from the hard service that was imposed on you]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **pain** and **turmoil**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from being hurt and from being troubled]

The expression **was imposed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Babylon. Alternate translation: [that Babylon imposed on you]

Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb, **was imposed**, and its object, **the hard service**, come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the slavery with which you were enslaved]

4.note: The taunters are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of amazement at the reversal of the oppressor’s power. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [At last the oppressor has ceased]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **insolence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The arrogant deeds have stopped]

Some ancient manuscripts read “The insolence.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “The hostility.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

5.note: The taunters are speaking as if the oppressive power of the wicked ruler were **the staff of the wicked**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the oppressive power of the wicked]

The terms **the staff of the wicked** and **the scepter of rulers** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the oppressive power of the wicked rulers]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in an angry way]
Here, **in nose** represents “anger.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in anger]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **persecution** and **restraint**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [unrestrainedly persecuting]

7.note: The taunters say **All of the earth** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [People throughout the earth rest, repose]

Here, **All of the earth** represents “all of the people of the earth.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All of the people of the earth rest, repose]

The terms **rests** and **reposes** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [reposes restfully]

The taunters are speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could break forth into singing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth sing for joy]

8.note: A direct quotation begins here without an explicit introductory word. The cypresses and cedars are speaking to the fallen king of Babylon. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

The taunters are speaking of **the cypresses** and **the cedars of Lebanon** as if they were living things that could exult. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Even the cypress trees and the cedars of Lebanon are safe now because of you]

9.note: The taunters are speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living thing that could tremble with anticipation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Those in Sheol far below are stirred with anticipation for your arrival]

The taunters are speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living thing that could awaken the dead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Raphaites there are awakened for you]

10.note: The point of this comparison is that just as the dead kings are weak and powerless, so the king of Babylon has now become weak and powerless. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [You also, you have become just as weak and powerless as we are]

The expression **you have been weakened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God has weakened you]

The expression **you have been likened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the observers in Sheol. Alternate translation: [God has made you to be like us]

11.note: The taunters are speaking as if the king of Babylon’s **pride** could physically descend to the place of the dead. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You, who were so proud, have been brought down to Sheol]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Your proud heart]

The expression **has been brought down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God has brought down]

The taunters are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Your pride has been brought down to Sheol along with the sound of your lyres]

The expression **is spread** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [spreads]

The taunters are speaking as if the worms consuming the king’s corpse were a blanket, calling them his **covering**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the worms are spread over you like a blanket]

12.note: The taunters are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of amazement at the dramatic reversal of the king of Babylon’s fortunes. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [What a fall you have taken from the heavens]

The taunters are speaking as if the king of Babylon’s loss of power were a literal fall, saying he has **fallen from the heavens**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [How completely you have lost all your power and greatness] or [How far you have fallen from your position of power]

The taunters are speaking as if the king of Babylon were a celestial body, calling him **morning star, son of the dawn**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you who shone like a star at dawn]

The taunters are speaking as if the king of Babylon were a tree that has been felled, saying he has been **cut down to the ground**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have been totally struck down to the ground, leaving not even a stump]

The expression **have been cut down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God has cut you down]

13.note: The pronoun **you** refers to the king of Babylon. The taunters state it emphatically to contrast the king’s grand ambitions with his actual downfall. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And you, king of Babylon, you said in your heart]

The taunters are speaking as if the king of Babylon’s intentions were words spoken inside his **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you thought to yourself]

The king of Babylon is speaking as if gaining supreme power were literally to **ascend** to the heavens. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will gain supreme power]

The king of Babylon is speaking as if having supreme authority were physically elevating his **throne above the stars of God**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make my authority greater than the authority of all of God’s heavenly beings]

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the Most High** has supreme authority over all, so the king of Babylon wants to have the same authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I will make myself equal to the Most High in supreme authority over all]

15.note: The word **But** introduces a contrast between what the king of Babylon boasted he would do in the previous verses and what has actually happened to him. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this outcome is the opposite of what the king intended. Alternate translation: [On the contrary,]

The taunters are speaking as if the king of Babylon’s utter defeat were a physical descent, saying he has been **brought down to Sheol**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have been brought down to the place of the dead]

The expression **have been brought down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you have fallen down] or [God has brought you down]

16.q: הֲ⁠זֶ֤ה הָ⁠אִישׁ֙ מַרְגִּ֣יז הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ מַרְעִ֖ישׁ מַמְלָכֽוֹת שָׂ֥ם תֵּבֵ֛ל כַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֖ר וְ⁠עָרָ֣י⁠ו הָרָ֑ס אֲסִירָ֖י⁠ו לֹא־פָ֥תַח בָּֽיְתָ⁠ה
16.note: The observers in Sheol are using the question form to express amazement and incredulity that this is the same man who once shook the earth. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is hard to believe that this is the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, who made the world like a wilderness and tore down its cities, who did not release his prisoners homeward!]

17.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a wilderness** is desolate and uninhabited, so the king of Babylon made the lands he conquered desolate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he who made the world desolate like a wilderness]

18.note: The taunters are speaking as if a tomb were **his house**. They mean that each king is buried in his own tomb. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each king in his own tomb]

19.note: Isaiah says that the Israelites will state the pronoun **you**, even though the verb translated as **you have been cast** will already include that meaning. They will do that because they will be contrasting what happens to the king of Assyria with what usually happens to other kings. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [But for your part, you have been cast from your grave]

Isaiah says that the Israelites will be speaking as if the king of Assyria had actually been dug up and **cast from** his **grave**. He means that this king will suffer the indignity of not being buried. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have been denied burial] or [no one has buried you]

The expression **you have been cast** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people have cast you]

The expressions **clothed** and **slain** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express these ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with people whom others have slain clothing you]

The taunters are speaking as if the dead bodies surrounding the king were a garment, saying he is **clothed** with the slain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [covered with the bodies of the slain] or [lying among the bodies of dead soldiers]

The taunters are using the participle **slain**, which functions here as an adjective, as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [with those whom others have slain]

The taunters are using the participle **pierced**, which functions here as an adjective, as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [whom others have pierced with their swords]

The taunters are using the participle **trampled**, which functions here as an adjective, as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [like a corpse that people have trampled]

20.note: The taunters are speaking as if the descendants of wicked rulers were **seed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of evildoers will not be remembered forever]

The expression **will not be named** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is people in general. Alternate translation: [People will never mention the offspring of evildoers]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for the preceding statement. The king of Babylon will not be buried with honor because he destroyed his own land and killed his own people. Alternate translation: [because]

21.q: הָכִ֧ינוּ לְ⁠בָנָ֛י⁠ו מַטְבֵּ֖חַ בַּ⁠עֲוֺ֣ן אֲבוֹתָ֑⁠ם בַּל־יָקֻ֨מוּ֙ וְ⁠יָ֣רְשׁוּ אָ֔רֶץ וּ⁠מָלְא֥וּ פְנֵֽי־תֵבֵ֖ל עָרִֽים
21.note: Here, **lest** indicates a negative purpose for what precedes it. The speaker commands the destruction of the king’s descendants so that they do not arise and take possession of the earth. See how the UST models this.

The pronoun **his** refers to the king of Babylon. The speaker shifts from addressing the king as “you” to referring to him in the third person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Prepare a slaughter for the king of Babylon’s sons]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the evil actions of their ancestors]

Here, **the face of the world** represents “the surface of the world.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the world]

22.note: The terms **name** and **remnant** and **offspring** and **posterity** are used together to mean that Babylon will be completely eliminated. Yahweh is using these terms together for emphasis. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [every trace and every survivor]

23.note: For poetic effect, Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb, **sweep**, and its indirect object, **broom**, come from the same root. Your language may have terms for this verb and object that come from the same root. If so, it would be appropriate to use them here in your translation. Alternate translation: [and I will sweep it with the sweeper of destruction]

Yahweh is speaking as if destroying Babylon were sweeping a floor with **the broom of destruction**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will completely destroy it]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will destroy it as if I were sweeping it away with a broom]

24.note: Yahweh is speaking as if his plan were only a hypothetical possibility by saying **If not**, but he means that it is actually true. He is using an oath formula to affirm with certainty that what he has planned will happen. If your language does not use the conditional form in this way, you could translate his words as a strong assertion. Alternate translation: [Surely, as I have intended, thus it shall be]

24.q: כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר דִּמִּ֨יתִי֙ כֵּ֣ן הָיָ֔תָה וְ⁠כַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָעַ֖צְתִּי הִ֥יא תָקֽוּם
24.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. See the UST.

25.note: Yahweh is speaking as if Assyria’s oppressive rule were **his yoke** placed on the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And his oppressive rule will be removed from them]

Yahweh is speaking as if Assyria’s forced labor were **his burden** placed upon the people’s shoulders. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will no longer have to perform forced labor for him]

26.note: Isaiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. See how the UST models this.

Here, **the hand** represents Yahweh’s power and action against the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his power extended over all of the nations]

The expression **stretched out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has stretched out]

27.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one can oppose what Yahweh has determined. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [and no one will thwart him!]
Here, **his hand** represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And his power is at work]

The expression **stretched out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh himself. Alternate translation: [And his hand he has stretched out]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one can resist Yahweh’s power once he has acted. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [and no one can turn it back!]

28.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **In the year of the death of King Ahaz** to introduce a new oracle. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the expression “burden” in [13:1](ta:13). Alternate translation: [this message]

29.note: Isaiah is speaking directly to **Philistia**, which is not present to hear him. This is a prophetic device for addressing a nation. If a speaker of your language would not do this, you could express this as a statement about Philistia. Alternate translation: [Philistia should not rejoice, none of them]

Isaiah is speaking as if the oppressor’s power were **the rod** that strikes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of the one who was striking you has ended]

The expression **is broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [that God broke the rod of the one striking you]

29.q: כִּֽי־מִ⁠שֹּׁ֤רֶשׁ נָחָשׁ֙ יֵ֣צֵא צֶ֔פַע וּ⁠פִרְי֖⁠וֹ שָׂרָ֥ף מְעוֹפֵֽף
29.note: Isaiah is speaking as if a succession of oppressive rulers were serpents, with each successor being more dangerous than the last. The first oppressor is called **the serpent**, and his successor is called **a viper**, and the final one is called **a flying serpent**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for from the first oppressor a worse oppressor will come, and his successor will be the most dangerous of all]

30.note: Isaiah is using **the firstborn of the poor** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the poorest of the poor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the poorest of the poor]

Some ancient manuscripts read “And the firstborn of the poor will graze.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “And the poor will graze in my pastures.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Yahweh is speaking as if the population of Philistia were a plant, calling their source **your root**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I will kill your people with famine]
The pronoun **it** refers to **famine**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and family will kill every one of your people]

31.note: Isaiah is speaking to the **gate** and the **city** as if they were people who could hear him. He is addressing inanimate objects to express the urgency of the coming destruction. If a speaker of your language would not do this, you could express this as a statement about the people in the city. Alternate translation: [Let the people at the gate wail and the people in the city cry out]

The expression **Be dissolved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who causes the action, the context indicates that it is the fear caused by the approaching enemy. Alternate translation: [Tremble in fear]

Isaiah is speaking as if the approaching army were **smoke** coming from the north. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the north an army is coming]

The pronoun **his** refers to the commander of the approaching army from the north. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and none in the army’s assembly is being separate]

32.note: Isaiah is using the question form to introduce the answer that follows. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And one will answer the messengers of a nation.]

Isaiah is speaking as if Zion were a physical shelter, saying the poor will **take refuge** in it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the poor of his people will be safe in it]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the poor of Yahweh’s people]
